title: An-Nisa, Al-Ma'idah, Al-Hujurat: Community, Justice, Peoples of the Book
bigQuestion: How do three Medinan surahs shape a community's duties to its own members, to justice, and to people of other faiths?

story.title: Nations and Tribes
story.kicker: One verse in a short surah says people were made into peoples so that they might know one another; readers keep returning to it.
paragraphs: In September 1893, Chicago hosted the World's Parliament of Religions beside the World's Columbian Exposition. Speakers from many faiths took the stage. Among them was Alexander Russell Webb, an American journalist and former diplomat who had become a Muslim. He was the main voice for Islam at the gathering, and he spent much of his speech answering what he saw as false pictures of the faith held by his audience.

More than a century later, the verse Muslims most often bring to such gatherings comes from a surah of only eighteen verses, Al-Hujurat, The Private Rooms. In Pickthall's translation: O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct. It is quoted on banners, at interfaith dinners and in graduation speeches in Illinois and around the world.

The verse did not arrive alone. Muslim tradition places Al-Hujurat in about 630, when delegations from across Arabia were coming to Medina. The verses before 49:13 tell the community not to mock one another, not to use insulting nicknames, not to spy or backbite. Commentators collected reports about the verse's occasion: one links it to a Black companion, Bilal, and the objections of Meccan nobles to his calling the prayer; another to a marriage proposal refused over lineage. The reports differ; the point they share is that lineage does not rank people.

Two longer surahs stand behind Al-Hujurat. An-Nisa, The Women, sets rules for orphans, inheritance and marriage, and tells believers to stand for justice even against themselves. Al-Ma'idah, The Table Spread, speaks of food, covenants, and Jews and Christians, and says God could have made all people one community but did not. Read together, the three surahs show a community working out who belongs, what it owes its members, and how it should treat those outside it. Those questions did not end in Medina. They were being asked in a Chicago hall in 1893, and they are asked in Chicago classrooms now.
story.think: What is the difference between a verse that says people should know one another and a verse that says they should agree? Which does 49:13 say?

lessons.title: Orphans and Inheritance
lessons.mainIdea: An-Nisa opens with the care of orphans and sets fixed shares of inheritance, including shares for women, in a society that had few such rules.
reading: Surah 4 is called *An-Nisa*, The Women, because so much of it concerns marriage, family and the rights of women and orphans. It has 176 ayahs and is the fourth-longest surah. Muslim tradition places it in Medina, with many verses dated to the years after the Battle of Uhud in about 625, when the community had lost men in battle and had many widows and orphans to provide for. Historians find that setting plausible: the surah's first ten verses are about orphans' property.

The surah opens by addressing all people, reminding them that they were created from a single soul. It then tells guardians to hand orphans their property when they come of age, not to swap good property for bad, and not to consume it wrongfully. Verse 10 warns that those who eat up orphans' wealth are eating fire. Commentators note that in the Arabia the sira describes, the strong often took what belonged to the weak, and these verses set limits.

Verses 11 and 12 give fixed *inheritance* shares. A son receives the share of two daughters; parents each receive one-sixth if the deceased has a child; a wife receives one-eighth if there are children and one-quarter if not; a husband one-quarter or one-half. Debts and bequests come first. Muslim jurists built a whole science, the *fara'id*, on these verses. Historians and many Muslim scholars note that giving daughters and wives fixed shares was a change in a society where women often inherited nothing. Modern Muslim writers debate the two-to-one ratio; some tie it to the husband's duty to support the family, others argue for rereading it, and the law schools have differed on details for centuries.

words.d: Surah 4, The Women; 176 ayahs; Medinan
property passed on at death; 4:11–12 set fixed shares for family members
the fixed shares of inheritance, and the branch of Islamic law that works them out
a battle near Medina in about 625 in which the Muslims lost many men

choices: Much of it concerns marriage, family and women's rights
check.why: The name comes from the surah's subject matter: orphans, marriage, inheritance and women's rights.

check.why: Tradition dates much of An-Nisa to after the Battle of Uhud, c. 625, when the community had to provide for orphans.

lessons.title: Marriage and a Hard Verse
lessons.mainIdea: An-Nisa's rules on marriage include verses that readers have debated intensely, above all 4:34; the debate is part of the tradition.
reading: Verse 4:3 is the Qur'an's main verse on the number of wives. It says that if a guardian fears he cannot deal justly with orphans, he may marry women of his choice, two, three or four, but if he fears he cannot treat them justly, then one. Commentators disagree about the link to orphans; some say the verse addresses guardians tempted to marry orphan girls for their wealth. Verse 129 adds that a man will not be able to deal equally between wives however he tries. Some modern scholars read 4:3 and 4:129 together as pointing toward one wife; classical jurists read 4:3 as permission with conditions.

Verse 4:34 is the most debated. It says men are *qawwamun* over women, a word Pickthall renders as in charge of, because of what God has given some over others and because men spend their wealth. It calls righteous women devoutly obedient. It then says that if a husband fears nushuz, a word usually translated as rebellion or ill-conduct, he should admonish, then leave the bed, then, in the Arabic, idribuhunna, usually translated strike them. The verse ends by saying that if they obey, no further way is to be sought against them.

Readers have handled this verse in many ways. Classical jurists set limits: hadith reports, paraphrased, say any striking must not cause harm, and many jurists said it was better not to strike at all. Modern Muslim scholars go further. Some read the Arabic verb in another of its meanings, to separate or to go away. Some argue the verse describes seventh-century Arabian households, not a rule for all time. Others keep the traditional reading and stress the limits. Muslim women scholars have written extensively on the verse since the 1990s. This course reports these readings; the disagreement is real and belongs to the tradition.

words.d: the word in 4:34 for men's role toward women; translated in charge of, maintainers, or protectors
the word in 4:34 usually translated as rebellion or ill-conduct; its meaning is debated
the classical traditions of Islamic law (such as Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali, Ja'fari) that read the same verses differently

look.title: Three Readers, One Verse
look.text: 4:34 says men are qawwamun over women. Reader A, a classical jurist: the verse sets a household order, with the husband responsible for support, and hadith limit the last step. Reader B, a modern scholar: the verse describes the households of its first hearers and its principles, responsibility and restraint, apply today without its details. Reader C, a modern woman scholar: the verb usually translated strike also means to leave or separate, and the whole Qur'an's stress on kindness between spouses should guide the choice.
look.prompt: What does each reader treat as the key to the verse: its words, its context, or the whole book? What would each need to show to persuade the others?

check.q: What condition does 4:3 attach to marrying more than one wife?
choices: The husband must be a merchant
The husband must be over forty
The husband must be able to treat them justly
check.why: 4:3 permits up to four wives but says one if a man fears he cannot deal justly.

check.q: Which word in 4:34 do modern scholars read in different senses?
check.why: Some modern readers take the Arabic verb as to separate or leave rather than to strike.

check.q: How did many classical jurists treat the last step in 4:34?
choices: They set limits and many said it was better not to strike at all
They made it the first step
check.why: Classical jurists, citing hadith, limited any striking to what causes no harm and often counseled against it.

lessons.title: Justice Against Yourself
lessons.mainIdea: An-Nisa 4:135 tells believers to stand firm for justice even against themselves and their families; it is one of the Qur'an's clearest ethical verses.
reading: Verse 4:135 opens: O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred. That is Pickthall's rendering. The verse goes on: whether the case is a rich man's or a poor man's, God is nearer to both; so do not follow passion lest you swerve. The Arabic word for justice here is *qist*, fair dealing, a word the Qur'an uses often. Muslim readers count the verse among the book's central statements on ethics, and it appears on courthouse walls and law-school seals in more than one country.

The verse is often read with a report about its occasion, collected by commentators: a dispute in Medina in which a Muslim accused a Jewish neighbor of theft, and the Prophet, according to the report, was warned by revelation not to side with his own community against the truth. The surah tells the story in 4:105–112 in general terms. Whether or not the report is exact, historians note that the verse addresses a community tempted to favor its own, and tells it not to.

The verse belongs to a cluster. Verse 4:58 tells believers to return trusts to their owners and to judge between people with justice. Verse 5:8, in the next surah, says that hatred of a people must not make you unjust. Jurists cite these verses for the rules of *testimony*: a witness must tell the truth even when it hurts. Modern Muslim writers cite them in debates about human rights. A student writing about justice in the Qur'an could do worse than to start with these three verses and their contexts.

words.d: fair dealing, justice; the word in 4:135 and 5:8
a witness's statement in a dispute; 4:135 says it must be truthful even against oneself
a tradition about the event a verse answered, collected by commentators and of varying reliability

look.title: Staunch in Justice

look.cite: Qur'an 4:135 (first part), An-Nisa, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: The verse names three people a witness might be tempted to protect. Why those three? What does the line about rich and poor add?

check.q: Against whom does 4:135 say a believer must be willing to testify?

check.why: Qist is the word for justice or fair dealing used in 4:135 and 5:8.

check.why: 5:8 says that hatred of a people must not make believers act unjustly, extending the rule to enemies.

lessons.title: Food and Covenant
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Ma'idah is among the last surahs by tradition; it sets food rules, declares the religion complete, and allows the food of the People of the Book.
reading: Surah 5, *Al-Ma'idah*, The Table Spread, has 120 ayahs. Its name comes from a story near its end (5:112–115) in which the disciples of Isa (Jesus) ask for a table of food to be sent from heaven. Muslim tradition counts it among the last surahs revealed, and many commentators place its opening verses at the Prophet's farewell pilgrimage in about 632. It opens with a command: O ye who believe! Fulfill your undertakings. Keeping agreements is a thread through the whole surah.

Verse 3 lists forbidden foods: carrion, blood, pork, and animals dedicated to anything other than God, with an exception for one forced by hunger. In the middle of the same verse comes a line Muslims hold dear: This day have I perfected your religion for you and completed My favor unto you, and have chosen for you as religion al-Islam, in Pickthall's words. Many commentators say this line came on the day of Arafat during the farewell pilgrimage; Shia commentators also connect nearby verses to the Prophet's words at Ghadir Khumm about Ali, a reading Sunni commentators do not share.

Verse 5 then widens the table. The food of those who received the Book before you, it says, is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them; and Muslim men may marry chaste women from among them. The phrase *People of the Book*, Ahl al-Kitab, means Jews and Christians, and by extension others with scriptures. Jurists built rules on this verse for kosher and other meat, for interfaith marriage and for shared meals. Muslims in Chicago who buy meat marked *halal*, permitted, or who eat with Jewish or Christian neighbors, are living inside these two verses.

words.d: Surah 5, The Table Spread; 120 ayahs; among the last revealed by tradition
Ahl al-Kitab; Jews and Christians, and others with a scripture, as the Qur'an calls them
permitted under Islamic law; often used of food

look.title: A Rule and an Opening
look.text: Verse 5:3 forbids carrion, blood, pork and animals dedicated to other than God. Verse 5:5 says the food of the People of the Book is lawful for Muslims, and Muslims' food is lawful for them, and permits marriage to their chaste women. A Muslim student in Chicago is invited to a Jewish friend's Sabbath dinner. Her family asks what the Qur'an says.
look.prompt: Using the two verses, what could she answer? Which questions would still need a scholar's help, and why might the law schools differ?

check.q: Where does Al-Ma'idah get its name?
choices: From a table the Prophet ate at

From a table of inheritance shares

check.why: 5:3 contains the line This day have I perfected your religion for you, tied by many to the farewell pilgrimage.

lessons.title: One Life, All Lives
lessons.mainIdea: Verse 5:32 says that killing one person is like killing all people and saving one is like saving all; readers ask what its context adds.
reading: Verse 5:32 follows the story of Adam's two sons, told in 5:27–31. One son kills the other, then learns from a raven how to bury him. The Qur'an does not name the sons; Muslim tradition calls them Habil and Qabil, the Bible's Abel and Cain. Then comes verse 32, in Pickthall's rendering: For that cause We decreed for the Children of Israel that whosoever killeth a human being for other than manslaughter or corruption in the earth, it shall be as if he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind.

Two things in the verse draw comment. First, it says the decree was given to the Children of Israel. Scholars have long noticed that the Mishnah, the early rabbinic code, contains a close parallel in tractate Sanhedrin 4:5, which says that one who destroys a single life is as if he destroyed a whole world, and one who saves a single life is as if he saved a whole world. Muslim commentators read the Qur'an as confirming an earlier teaching; historians read the parallel as evidence of shared traditions in late-antique Arabia.

Second, the verse has two *exceptions*: for other than manslaughter, that is, as punishment for murder, and corruption in the earth. The next verse, 5:33, sets severe punishments for those who wage war against God and His Messenger and spread corruption. Classical jurists read 5:33 as the law against armed brigandage, hirabah. Modern Muslim scholars cite 5:32 against terrorism and note that those who kill civilians fall under the corruption the verse condemns, not outside it. Readers who quote only the first half of the verse, or only the exceptions, each miss part of it.

words.d: the names Muslim tradition gives Adam's two sons, the Bible's Abel and Cain
a case a rule sets aside; 5:32 names two
armed brigandage or waging war on society; the crime jurists read in 5:33
the early rabbinic law code, compiled c. 200 CE, with a parallel to 5:32 in Sanhedrin 4:5

look.cite: Qur'an 5:32, Al-Ma'idah, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: Compare this verse with Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5. What is the same? What does the Qur'an's version add, and why might it say the decree was given to the Children of Israel?

check.q: What story comes right before 5:32?
choices: Adam's two sons, one of whom kills the other
check.why: 5:27–31 tells of the two sons of Adam; verse 32 draws its lesson from that killing.

check.q: Which text has a close parallel to 5:32?

check.q: How do modern Muslim scholars use 5:32 in debates about terrorism?

lessons.title: To Each a Law and a Way
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Ma'idah speaks of Jews and Christians in more than one tone, and 5:48 says God could have made all people one community but chose to test them in their differences.
reading: Al-Ma'idah speaks about Jews and Christians more than any other surah, and not in one voice. Verses 44–47 say the Torah and the Gospel contain guidance and light and tell each people to judge by what God sent down to them. Verse 51 tells believers not to take Jews and Christians as *awliya*, a word translated as friends, allies or protectors. Verse 69 says Jews, Sabians and Christians who believe in God and the last day and do right have nothing to fear. Verse 82 says those nearest in affection to the believers are those who say We are Christians, because among them are priests and monks who are not proud.

Commentators handle these verses by asking their occasions. Many, from al-Tabari on, tie 5:51 to political alliances during the conflicts of Medina, when some Muslims kept protective pacts with tribes at war with the community; on this reading the verse concerns wartime loyalty, not friendship in general. Others read it more broadly. Modern Muslim scholars generally stress the first reading and point to 60:8, which says God does not forbid kindness and fairness to those who have not fought the believers over religion.

Verse 48 gathers the surah's thinking. In Pickthall's rendering: For each We have appointed a divine law and a traced-out way. Had Allah willed He could have made you one community. But that He may try you by that which He hath given you (He hath made you as ye are). So vie one with another in good works. Classical commentators mostly read the verse as describing the succession of laws, each people in its time; many modern readers, Muslim and not, read it as the Qur'an's own account of religious *diversity*, difference as a test and a call to compete in good. Both readings have the text on their side; the second has become common at interfaith gatherings.

words.d: friends, allies or protectors; the debated word in 5:51
difference among peoples and faiths; 5:48 presents it as willed by God and as a test
Tawrat and Injil; the scriptures the Qur'an says were given to Musa and Isa

look.title: Had Allah Willed
look.text: For each We have appointed a divine law and a traced-out way. Had Allah willed He could have made you one community. But that He may try you by that which He hath given you (He hath made you as ye are). So vie one with another in good works. Unto Allah ye will all return, and He will then inform you of that wherein ye differ.
look.cite: Qur'an 5:48 (part), Al-Ma'idah, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: The verse says differences will be explained on the last day, not now. What does that leave for people to do in the meantime, according to the text?

choices: Wartime alliances during the conflicts of Medina
check.why: From al-Tabari on, many tie the verse on awliya to protective pacts with tribes at war with the community.

lessons.title: Manners for a Community
lessons.mainIdea: Al-Hujurat, a short surah of about 630, gives rules of conduct: verify news, make peace, do not mock, do not spy, do not backbite.
reading: Surah 49, *Al-Hujurat*, The Private Rooms, has eighteen ayahs. The name comes from verse 4, which rebukes people who shouted to the Prophet from outside the rooms where his wives lived. Muslim tradition dates the surah to about 630, the ninth year after the move to Medina, when delegations from Arabian tribes were arriving to make terms. Historians accept that setting as consistent with the surah's concerns: how a growing and mixed community should behave.

The first verses set manners toward the Prophet: do not raise your voices above his, do not shout for him from outside. Verse 6 gives a rule that Muslim ethicists quote often: if a wrongdoer brings you news, check it, lest you harm a people in ignorance. Verses 9 and 10 turn to conflict inside the community: if two groups of believers fight, make peace between them, and if one goes on wronging the other, fight the one that wrongs until it returns; the believers are brothers, so make peace between your brothers.

Verses 11 and 12 are about everyday harm. Do not let a people mock another people, who may be better than they; do not let women mock women; do not insult one another or use offensive nicknames. Avoid much suspicion, for some suspicion is a sin. Do not spy. Do not *backbite*: would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? The image is meant to disgust. Teachers in Muslim schools use these two verses for lessons on bullying, and their plain language is one reason the surah is a favorite for memorization.

words.d: Surah 49, The Private Rooms; 18 ayahs; dated by tradition to about 630
to speak ill of someone who is not present; forbidden in 49:12
groups sent by Arabian tribes to Medina around 630 to make terms; the year of delegations

look.title: Suspicion, Spying, Backbiting
look.text: Paraphrase of 49:11–12: Believers, let no people mock another people, who may be better than they, nor women mock women. Do not find fault with one another or call one another by insulting names. Avoid much suspicion, for some suspicion is sin. Do not spy on one another, and do not speak ill of one another behind their backs. Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would hate it.
look.cite: Qur'an 49:11–12, Al-Hujurat, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: The passage moves from public mocking to private suspicion to words said behind someone's back. Why that order? What is the image of the dead brother doing?

check.q: What does 49:6 tell believers to do when a wrongdoer brings news?
check.why: 49:6 says to verify news from an unreliable source, lest you harm people in ignorance.

check.q: What does 49:9 say to do if two groups of believers fight?
check.why: 49:9–10 tell the community to make peace between fighting believers, who are called brothers.

check.q: What image does 49:12 use for backbiting?
choices: Eating the flesh of a dead brother
A bird with a broken wing
check.why: The verse asks whether anyone would want to eat his dead brother's flesh, an image meant to disgust.

lessons.title: That You May Know One Another
lessons.mainIdea: Verse 49:13 says God made people into nations and tribes to know one another, and that the noblest is the best in conduct; it is the Qur'an's most-quoted verse on human difference.
reading: Verse 13 changes address. The surah has been speaking to the believers; now it says O mankind. In Pickthall's translation: We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct. The Arabic behind best in conduct is atqakum, the one with most *taqwa*, mindfulness of God. The verse ends: God is Knower, Aware.

Commentators give several occasion reports. One says that at the conquest of Mecca in about 630, Bilal, a formerly enslaved Black companion, gave the call to prayer from the roof of the Ka'bah, and some Meccan nobles objected; the verse answered them. Another concerns a marriage proposal refused because of the suitor's lineage. Al-Tabari and later commentators note that the reports differ, and they draw the same lesson from all of them: in the Qur'an's view, *lineage*, one's descent and tribe, confers no rank. Hadith reports, paraphrased, have the Prophet saying in his farewell sermon that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab to an Arab, except by taqwa.

The verse has a long afterlife. Sufi writers read knowing one another as a stage on the path to knowing God. Modern Muslim scholars cite it against racism and tribalism, and it was quoted during the American civil rights era by Muslim leaders, including Malcolm X after his pilgrimage in 1964. It appears at interfaith gatherings in Chicago and on the walls of Islamic schools in Illinois. Some readers caution that the verse is about knowing, not agreeing: it does not say all religions are the same, and the surah around it is written for a particular community. Both points are in the text.

words.d: mindfulness of God; the measure of nobility in 49:13
descent from a family or tribe; 49:13 is read as denying it any rank
a formerly enslaved companion of the Prophet, the first to give the call to prayer

look.title: Nations and Tribes
look.text: O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct. Lo! Allah is Knower, Aware.
look.cite: Qur'an 49:13, Al-Hujurat, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930)
look.prompt: The verse gives a purpose for difference and a measure of worth. State each in your own words. What does the verse not say?

check.q: Whom does 49:13 address?
check.why: 49:13 shifts from O ye who believe to O mankind, addressing all people.

check.q: According to 49:13, what makes a person noblest in God's sight?
check.why: Pickthall's best in conduct renders atqakum, the one with the most taqwa.

check.q: What do commentators agree on, though their occasion reports differ?
choices: The verse was revealed in Mecca before the hijra
check.why: Whether the report concerns Bilal or a marriage proposal, the lesson drawn is that descent gives no rank.

lessons.title: Context and Occasion
lessons.mainIdea: Classical commentators read Medinan verses through reports of their occasions; historians weigh those reports and set the surahs in the years 622 to 632.
reading: Every lesson in this chapter has leaned on two tools. The first is *asbab al-nuzul*, the occasions of revelation: reports, passed down and collected by scholars such as al-Wahidi in the eleventh century, about the event a verse answered. The second is the sira, the traditional life of the Prophet, which gives the order of events in Medina: the arrival in 622, Badr in about 624, Uhud in about 625, the treaty with Mecca at Hudaybiyyah in about 628, the conquest of Mecca in about 630, the delegations, and the farewell pilgrimage in about 632.

Historians use both with care. The sira in the form we have was written down in the eighth and ninth centuries, more than a hundred years after the events. Occasion reports often conflict, as we saw for 49:13, and some were plainly guesses. Modern scholars, Muslim and non-Muslim, agree that the Qur'an itself is the earliest source, and that the reports help most when several independent ones agree, or when the verse's own wording supports them. Where reports disagree, this course has said so.

Why does it matter? Because the three surahs in this chapter contain the verses most often quoted about other faiths, about women and about violence, both by Muslims and by critics of Islam. A verse read without its occasion can be made to say almost anything. A verse read with its occasion, its neighbors and the rest of the book is harder to twist. That is the argument Muslim commentators made a thousand years ago, and it is the argument historians make today, for different reasons.

words.d: occasions of revelation; reports about the events that verses answered
the treaty between the Muslims and Mecca in about 628
the Prophet's last hajj, in about 632, to which tradition ties parts of Al-Ma'idah

look.title: Medina in Ten Years

choices: Reports about the events that verses answered
The thirty parts of the Qur'an

choices: It was written down more than a century after the events

lessons.title: Classical and Modern Readers
lessons.mainIdea: On the verses about other faiths, classical commentators and modern scholars often reach different emphases from the same text; both belong to the Muslim tradition of reading.
reading: Put the verses side by side. 2:62 and 5:69 say Jews, Christians and Sabians who believe in God and the last day and do right have their reward. 2:256 says there is no compulsion in religion. 5:48 says God could have made all people one community. 49:13 says nations and tribes exist to know one another. Against these stand 5:51 on not taking Jews and Christians as awliya, 3:85 on no religion other than islam being accepted, and the fighting verses of Surah 9. Every serious reader has to say how these fit together.

Classical commentators mostly used two tools. One was *abrogation*, naskh: a later verse can set aside an earlier ruling. Some applied it widely, holding that the Surah 9 verses replaced the gentler ones; many applied it narrowly or not at all. The other was specification: reading a verse as about the people it was revealed about. Ibn Kathir, for example, read 2:62 as about people before Muhammad's time, while al-Tabari recorded readings on both sides. Most classical readers also assumed a world of Muslim rule with protected non-Muslim communities, the dhimma system, and read the verses in that light.

Modern Muslim scholars, writing in a world of nation-states and religious pluralism, have shifted emphasis. Many argue that abrogation was overused and that the fighting verses address specific enemies. Many read 5:48 and 49:13 as the Qur'an's own charter for living among other faiths. Some, in the *pluralist* camp, go further and read 2:62 as promising reward to righteous Jews and Christians today; others hold the older line that the verse's promise ended with Muhammad's coming. Non-Muslim historians add a third voice, describing the seventh-century setting and declining to say which reading is right. This course does the same.

words.d: naskh; the classical theory that a later verse can set aside an earlier ruling
the classical system under which non-Muslims lived as protected communities under Muslim rule
a reader who holds that the Qur'an promises reward to righteous people of other faiths

look.title: Two Verses, Two Readers
look.text: Verse 2:62 (and 5:69) says those who believe, and Jews, Christians and Sabians who believe in God and the last day and do right, have their reward and nothing to fear. Verse 3:85 says whoever seeks a religion other than islam, it will not be accepted. Ibn Kathir (d. 1373) read 2:62 as about people who lived before Muhammad and 3:85 as governing now. Some modern scholars read islam in 3:85 as submission to God in any tradition, and 2:62 as a standing promise.
look.prompt: What must each reader do with the verse that does not fit his reading? What would a historian say about the first hearers of each verse?

check.q: What is naskh, or abrogation?
choices: The theory that a later verse can set aside an earlier ruling
check.why: Abrogation is the classical idea that some verses replace earlier rulings; scholars disagree on how widely it applies.

check.q: How did Ibn Kathir read 2:62?
choices: As about people who lived before Muhammad's time
As a promise to righteous Jews and Christians of every age
check.why: Ibn Kathir specified 2:62 to earlier communities, while al-Tabari recorded readings on both sides.

check.q: What do non-Muslim historians add to the debate over these verses?
choices: A ruling on which reading is true
A description of the seventh-century setting, without ruling on truth
A new translation that settles the matter
A claim that the verses are not in the Qur'an
check.why: Historians describe the setting and the readings and decline to judge which reading is right.

review.q: Which subject fills the opening verses of An-Nisa?
review.why: An-Nisa 4:1–12 deal with orphans, their property, and fixed shares of inheritance.

review.q: What does 4:135 require of a witness?
choices: To testify only in a mosque
To be staunch in justice even against oneself or one's parents
review.why: 4:135 tells believers to stand for justice as witnesses for God, even against themselves and their kin.

review.q: Which verse permits Muslims to eat the food of the People of the Book?
review.why: 5:5 declares the food of those given the Book lawful and permits marriage to their chaste women.

review.q: What do readers who quote only the first half of 5:32 leave out?
choices: The two exceptions and the next verse on corruption
review.why: 5:32 names exceptions for murder and corruption in the earth, and 5:33 sets punishments for those who spread corruption.

review.q: In 5:48, what reason does the text give for God not making all people one community?
choices: Because the earth is too large
To test them in what He gave them
review.why: 5:48 says God could have made people one community but tests them by what He has given, so they should compete in good works.

review.q: Which of these is forbidden in 49:12?
review.why: 49:12 forbids much suspicion, spying and backbiting, with the image of eating a dead brother's flesh.

review.q: What is the measure of nobility in 49:13?
review.why: The verse says the noblest in God's sight is the one with the most taqwa, Pickthall's best in conduct.

review.q: How do many modern Muslim scholars differ from many classical ones on 5:51?
choices: They say it forbids all friendship
They stress that it concerned wartime alliances, not friendship in general
They say it is about food
They remove it from the Qur'an
review.why: Modern scholars mostly read 5:51 through its occasion in Medina's conflicts and pair it with 60:8 on kindness to those who do not fight.
